subtopics.name: Aging process and older adult health

questions.stem: A 15-year-old in the hospital for 2 weeks after a car crash dyes their hair a new color each visit, tries on different styles of dress and says, "I don't know who I want to be." According to Erikson, which developmental task is the teen working on?

options.text: Identity versus role confusion
Trust versus mistrust
Industry versus inferiority
Intimacy versus isolation

rationale.correct: Erikson: trust (infant), autonomy (toddler), initiative (preschool), industry (school age), identity (adolescent), intimacy (young adult), generativity (middle adult), integrity (older adult).

perOption.a: Adolescents try out roles and styles while forming a sense of self.
perOption.b: This is the task of infancy.
perOption.c: This is the task of school-age children.
perOption.d: This is the task of young adulthood.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old resident of an assisted living facility enjoys telling staff about raising a family and working as a teacher. The resident sometimes says, "I did my best." Which nursing intervention supports this resident's developmental task?

options.text: Encourage reminiscence and a life review with photos
Steer conversations to current events instead of the past
Discourage long stories about the past during care
Suggest the resident take a class to start a new career

rationale.correct: Older adults work toward integrity; reminiscence and life review support it.

perOption.a: Reviewing life supports integrity rather than despair.
perOption.b: This discourages a healthy developmental process.
perOption.d: This is not the developmental focus.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support ego integrity in older adults.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old client at a wellness visit says, "I coach my daughter's soccer team, I mentor new staff at work, and I volunteer on weekends. It feels good to give back." Which developmental task does this reflect?

options.text: Generativity versus stagnation
Intimacy versus isolation
Identity versus role confusion
Integrity versus despair

rationale.correct: Middle adulthood: generativity, contributing to others and to the next generation.

perOption.a: Middle adults focus on guiding the next generation and contributing to others.
perOption.b: This is the task of young adulthood.
perOption.c: This is the task of adolescence.
perOption.d: This is the task of older adulthood.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client at a clinic visit is accompanied by an adult child who lists several changes noticed over the past year. Which findings are expected changes of normal aging? Select all that apply.

options.text: Thinner, less elastic skin
Needing reading glasses for close work
Trouble hearing high-pitched voices
Feeling less thirsty than before
Sudden confusion that began yesterday
New leaking of urine when coughing

rationale.correct: Know normal aging and the findings that need evaluation, such as delirium or incontinence.

perOption.a: Collagen and elastin decrease with age.
perOption.b: The lens becomes less flexible (presbyopia).
perOption.c: Age-related hearing loss affects high frequencies.
perOption.d: Thirst sensation falls, raising the risk of dehydration.
perOption.e: Acute confusion is not normal aging and suggests delirium.
perOption.f: Bladder capacity falls with age, but incontinence is not normal and needs evaluation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 79-year-old client with mild hearing loss and cataracts how to use a new inhaler. Which teaching approach is best?

options.text: Short, unhurried sessions, large print and a demonstration
One long session that covers everything about the inhaler at once
Speaking quickly so that the client stays interested and alert
A detailed handout printed in small type

rationale.correct: Adapt teaching to sensory and cognitive changes in older adults: slow pace, short sessions, large print and demonstration.

perOption.a: This accommodates changes in vision, hearing and processing speed.
perOption.b: This overwhelms the learner.
perOption.d: Vision changes make small print hard to read.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client who is 28 weeks pregnant with her second child received Tdap during her first pregnancy 3 years ago. She asks whether she needs any vaccines now. What is the nurse's response?

options.text: "Tdap again in this pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks."
"You don't need Tdap this time, because you had it 3 years ago."
"An MMR booster, to protect the baby from measles."
"Vaccines are not given to people who are pregnant."

rationale.correct: In pregnancy: Tdap in each pregnancy (27 to 36 weeks) and inactivated influenza; avoid live vaccines.

perOption.a: Tdap is given in every pregnancy to pass pertussis antibodies to the newborn.
perOption.b: Tdap is repeated with each pregnancy.
perOption.c: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy.
perOption.d: Tdap and inactivated influenza are recommended.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Four adults at a community clinic are due for the MMR vaccine. Which client should the nurse not vaccinate today?

options.text: A 28-year-old who is 10 weeks pregnant
A 30-year-old with a runny nose and no fever
A 32-year-old who is breastfeeding a 2-month-old
A 25-year-old with a history of hives from eggs

rationale.correct: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, live intranasal influenza) are avoided in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression.

perOption.a: MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
perOption.b: A mild illness is not a contraindication.
perOption.d: Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A parent brings a 6-month-old for scheduled vaccines. The nurse is reviewing the history. Which finding is a true contraindication to giving the DTaP vaccine today?

options.text: Anaphylaxis within minutes of the previous DTaP dose
A runny nose and a temperature of 37.8 °C (100 °F) today
A red, sore thigh for 2 days after the last vaccine
A current course of amoxicillin for an ear infection

rationale.correct: True contraindications are uncommon; avoid missed opportunities to vaccinate.

perOption.a: A severe allergic reaction to a previous dose is a contraindication.
perOption.b: A mild illness is not a contraindication.
perOption.d: Taking an antibiotic is not a contraindication.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A healthy child who is up to date on all vaccines through 6 months comes for a 12-month well-child visit. Which vaccines should the nurse expect to give?

options.text: The first doses of MMR and varicella
The hepatitis B dose that is given at birth
The first dose of the HPV vaccine series
A Tdap booster for pertussis protection

rationale.correct: Key schedule points: hepatitis B at birth; DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV and rotavirus at 2, 4 and 6 months; MMR and varicella at 12 to 15 months.

perOption.a: MMR and varicella are first given at 12 to 15 months.
perOption.b: This is given at birth.
perOption.c: HPV is given at 9 to 12 years.
perOption.d: Tdap is given at 11 to 12 years.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A healthy 55-year-old client who had chickenpox as a child and shingles 2 years ago asks about the shingles vaccine. What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "The recombinant vaccine is advised at 50 and over, as 2 doses."
"You don't need it now, because you've already had shingles once."
"One dose of the vaccine gives you protection for life."
"The shingles vaccine is meant for children."

rationale.correct: Recombinant zoster vaccine: 2 doses for adults 50 and older (and some younger immunocompromised adults), including after shingles.

perOption.a: Recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for adults 50 and older, even after shingles.
perOption.b: It is recommended whether or not the person has had shingles.
perOption.d: It is for adults.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse is screening several healthy, full-term infants of different ages at their well-child visits and explaining to the parents what to expect next. For each milestone, choose the age by which it usually appears.

rationale.correct: Use milestones to screen development, and refer when they are delayed.

perOption.r1:c1: The social smile appears at about 2 months.
perOption.r2:c2: Infants usually sit unsupported by 6 to 8 months.
perOption.r3:c3: The pincer grasp develops around 9 to 10 months.
perOption.r4:c3: This is early for most infants.
perOption.r4:c4: Independent walking usually starts at 12 to 15 months.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A full-term infant weighed 3.5 kg at birth and is breastfeeding well. The parent asks what the baby should weigh at the 12-month visit. Using the usual pattern of infant weight gain, about how many kilograms should the nurse expect the infant to weigh at 12 months?

rationale.correct: Birth weight usually triples by 12 months: 3.5 × 3 = 10.5 kg. It doubles by about 5 to 6 months.
references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The parent of a 2-year-old says, "She throws herself on the floor and screams when I say no. I've started giving her the candy to stop it." What is the nurse's best advice?

options.text: "Keep her safe, ignore the tantrum, then praise calm behavior."
"A quick spank will teach her that tantrums don't work."
"Keep giving her the candy, since it ends the tantrum quickly."
"Put her alone in a locked room until she calms down."

rationale.correct: Toddlers: autonomy versus shame; use consistent limits, simple choices and ignoring the tantrum when it is safe.

perOption.a: Ignoring tantrums while keeping the child safe reduces them; toddlers are seeking autonomy.
perOption.b: Physical punishment is not recommended.
perOption.d: This is unsafe.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old is scheduled for a tonsillectomy tomorrow morning and asks the nurse, "Will they cut my whole neck off?" Which approach best prepares the child?

options.text: Use a doll to show what will happen, close to the procedure
Give a detailed explanation using the words the surgeon will use
Avoid answering so that the child is not frightened further
Show the child diagrams of the throat and tonsils

rationale.correct: Preschoolers: magical thinking and fear of bodily injury; use play and simple, honest explanations shortly before procedures.

perOption.a: Preschoolers learn through play and fear bodily injury; preparation close to the event works best.
perOption.b: Medical words are too abstract and can increase fear.
perOption.d: Diagrams are too abstract for a preschooler.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prepare a preschooler for a procedure.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old in traction for a femur fracture will be in the hospital for 3 weeks and says, "I'm bored." Which activity is most appropriate?

options.text: A board game with rules, or building a model kit
A soft rattle and a set of brightly colored rings
A push-pull toy to use beside the bed
A baby doll with a bottle and blanket

rationale.correct: School-age children: industry, rule-based games, collections and projects.

perOption.a: School-age children enjoy rule-based games and finishing projects (industry).
perOption.b: These suit infants.
perOption.c: This suits toddlers and needs walking.
perOption.d: This suits younger children.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose an activity for a school-age child.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old comes to the clinic with a parent for a sports physical. The teen answers questions in a few words and keeps looking at the parent. Which approach should the nurse take for the health history?

options.text: Interview the teen alone for part of the visit, with privacy limits
Ask the parent to answer the questions, since the teen is quiet
Tell the teen that everything said will be shared with the parent
Skip questions about sex and substance use with the parent present

rationale.correct: Adolescents: privacy, confidentiality with its limits, and screening for risk behaviors (HEEADSSS).

perOption.a: Privacy encourages honest disclosure about risk behaviors, and teens need to know what must be shared.
perOption.b: Adolescents should be engaged directly.
perOption.d: These questions are essential and are asked privately.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The parent of a 15-month-old who weighs 11 kg asks whether it is time to turn the car seat to face forward, because the child's legs touch the back seat. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Keep it rear-facing until your child reaches the seat's limit."
"Turn it around now, since your child is older than 1 year."
"Turn it once the legs are bent, since that must be uncomfortable."
"Turn it around whenever your child starts to complain."

rationale.correct: Rear-facing car seats protect the head and neck; keep children rear-facing to the seat's limits.

perOption.a: Rear-facing is safest; current guidance is to stay rear-facing to the seat's height or weight limit.
perOption.b: Turning at 1 year is not recommended.
perOption.c: Bent legs are safe; this is not a reason to turn the seat.
perOption.d: Safety, not complaints, guides the decision.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Before discharge, the nurse reviews safe sleep with the parents of a healthy 2-day-old. Which statement by a parent shows correct understanding?

options.text: "We'll put the baby on the back on a firm mattress in an empty crib."
"We'll put the baby on the tummy so that the baby won't choke on spit-up."
"We'll put soft bumpers and a pillow around the baby for comfort."
"The baby will sleep in our bed each night so we can hear breathing."

rationale.correct: Safe sleep: on the back, on a firm flat surface, in an empty crib, with room-sharing but not bed-sharing.

perOption.a: This reduces the risk of SIDS and suffocation.
perOption.b: Prone sleep increases SIDS risk.
perOption.d: Bed-sharing increases risk; room-sharing without bed-sharing is advised.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A clinic nurse is deciding which children to screen for lead poisoning. Which child is at highest risk?

options.text: A 2-year-old living in a 1950 house with peeling window paint
A 10-year-old who moved into a newly built apartment last year
A 6-month-old who is breastfed and lives in a new home
A 16-year-old who plays soccer after school

rationale.correct: Lead risk: homes built before 1978, hand-to-mouth behavior and some imported products; screen high-risk toddlers.

perOption.a: Older homes may have lead paint, and toddlers put things in their mouths.
perOption.b: This child is at lower risk.
perOption.c: This infant is at lower risk.
perOption.d: This is not a main risk.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse has finished teaching a client how to give enoxaparin injections at home. What is the best way for the nurse to confirm that the client has understood?

options.text: Have the client show the injection steps on a practice pad
Ask the client, "Do you understand how to give the injection?"
Give the client a printed handout with pictures of the steps
Have a family member sign the discharge teaching form

rationale.correct: Teach-back and return demonstration are the best ways to confirm understanding.

perOption.a: A return demonstration shows real understanding of a skill.
perOption.b: Clients often say yes without understanding.
perOption.d: A signature does not confirm understanding.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the second day after an abdominal hysterectomy, a client needs teaching about incision care before discharge tomorrow. The client received IV morphine 15 minutes ago for pain of 8 out of 10. When is the client most ready to learn?

options.text: Later today, when the pain is controlled and the client is alert
Right now, while the morphine is having its strongest effect
Right now, before the pain medicine has had any time to start working
Tomorrow, in the hour before the client leaves the hospital

rationale.correct: Assess readiness to learn: comfort, alertness and motivation.

perOption.a: Readiness to learn needs comfort and attention.
perOption.b: Opioid sedation impairs learning.
perOption.d: This leaves too little time for practice and questions.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old client who smokes a pack a day says, "I know I really should quit, and I've been thinking about it. Maybe after the holidays in a few months." Which stage of change is this client in?

options.text: Contemplation
Precontemplation
Preparation
Action

rationale.correct: Stages of change: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance.

perOption.a: The client is thinking about change within about 6 months but has no firm plan.
perOption.b: The client would have no intention of changing.
perOption.c: The client would be planning to act within a month.
perOption.d: The client would already be changing.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify a client's stage of change.

questions.stem: A client who reads at about a third-grade level is going home on warfarin. Which teaching strategy is best?

options.text: Plain words, short sentences and pictures of the key points
Medical terms, so that the information about the drug is accurate
The full drug leaflet to read at home later
A quick talk that covers as much as possible

rationale.correct: Use plain language, focus on 2 or 3 key points and confirm with teach-back.

perOption.a: Clear, simple information improves understanding.
perOption.b: Jargon reduces understanding.
perOption.c: Long text may not be understood.
perOption.d: Speed reduces understanding.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach clients with limited health literacy.

questions.stem: A healthy 40-year-old office worker asks how much exercise is recommended each week. What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: 150 minutes of moderate activity plus strength work twice a week
One 30-minute walk on the weekend is enough for good health at this age
Strength training alone, with no need for aerobic activity
Daily marathon-style training to get the full benefit

rationale.correct: Adults: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus strength training on 2 days.

perOption.a: This is the national guideline for adults.
perOption.b: This is too little.
perOption.d: This is not the general recommendation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.
